content: Byssinosis is a pulmonary condition caused by the inhalation of cotton dust or dust from other vegetable fibers such as flax, hemp, or sisal, typically in occupational settings. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP), also referred to as extrinsic allergic alveolitis (EAA), is not a singular disease but rather a complex syndrome with varying degrees of severity, clinical manifestations, and natural progression. The syndrome was first identified in Iceland in 1874 and was initially termed heykatarr. The pathophysiology of hypersensitivity pneumonitis involves sensitization due to repeated inhalation of organic dusts containing one of over 300 known antigens. Commonly recognized forms of the disease include farmer's lung and bird fancier's lung. The etiology of hypersensitivity pneumonitis may involve exposure to specific organic antigens, but no single genetic mutation or definitive cause has been established. Differentiating hypersensitivity pneumonitis from other diseases is essential, as it shares overlapping symptoms with other pulmonary conditions. The global prevalence of hypersensitivity pneumonitis is estimated to be approximately a few cases per 100,000 individuals. Incidence rates vary by region and occupational exposure. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis can affect individuals of all age groups, though it is more commonly observed in middle-aged adults. Both men and women are equally susceptible to the condition, with no significant gender predilection. There is no racial predisposition to hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and it typically affects individuals regardless of ethnicity. Risk factors for developing hypersensitivity pneumonitis include occupational or environmental exposure to organic dusts, such as those encountered in farming, bird breeding, or other industries involving organic materials. The natural history of hypersensitivity pneumonitis varies. Many patients remain asymptomatic, while others may develop early clinical features such as cough, dyspnea, or fatigue. If left untreated, the condition can progress to chronic forms, leading to irreversible lung damage, including pulmonary fibrosis. Common complications include respiratory failure and chronic lung disease. Prognosis is generally favorable with early diagnosis and avoidance of antigen exposure, but delayed treatment can result in poorer outcomes. The diagnosis of hypersensitivity pneumonitis is based on meeting specific diagnostic criteria, which include clinical history, exposure history, and supportive findings from imaging or laboratory studies. Symptoms of hypersensitivity pneumonitis may include cough, shortness of breath, fatigue, and fever, though many patients may initially be asymptomatic. Physical examination findings in hypersensitivity pneumonitis are often nonspecific but may include crackles or wheezing on auscultation. There are no specific laboratory findings unique to hypersensitivity pneumonitis. However, elevated serum precipitins against specific antigens may support the diagnosis. Other laboratory findings may include elevated inflammatory markers or hypoxemia. Imaging studies, particularly high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT), are the modality of choice for evaluating hypersensitivity pneumonitis. HRCT findings may include ground-glass opacities, centrilobular nodules, or fibrosis in chronic cases. Other diagnostic studies, such as pulmonary function tests, may reveal restrictive lung patterns or reduced diffusion capacity. Bronchoalveolar lavage or lung biopsy may also aid in diagnosis by demonstrating lymphocytic inflammation or granulomas. There is no definitive cure for hypersensitivity pneumonitis. The cornerstone of management is the avoidance of antigen exposure and supportive care. In some cases, corticosteroids may be used to reduce inflammation, particularly in acute or subacute forms of the disease.
